Question: Describe target architecture for enterprise-scale: active-active or active-passive across regions, RPO/RTO commitments, failover automation, blast radius of single-component failure.
Response: Target architecture: active-passive across Azure paired regions with active-active within a region (availability zones). RPO: near-zero for workflow state (Cosmos DB continuous backup with geo-replication) and for MAF graph checkpoints (preserved across DF replay via the MAF Durable Task extension). RTO: <5 minutes via automated failover (Azure Traffic Manager for APIM, Cosmos DB automatic failover, Durable Functions checkpoint replay in secondary region). Blast radius containment maps to the three execution layers. (1) Single agent executor (GHCP SDK session) failure — ephemeral, only the executor node is affected; MAF re-runs the executor within its graph lifecycle. (2) Single MAF executor or validator failure — MAF pause/resume handles it; typed error can route to a fallback conditional edge. (3) Single Hosted Agent container failure — Foundry restarts the container; in-flight sessions are lost but MAF checkpoint + DF state persist; the next session picks up from last checkpoint. (4) Single MCP tool failure — APIM circuit breaker activates. (5) Region failure — Traffic Manager routes to paired region; Cosmos DB serves from secondary; DF replays from geo-replicated checkpoints; MAF graph state is restored via the Durable Task extension; Fleet Manager in the secondary region takes over. No single component failure cascades across the fleet. Runtime isolation: all backends on Private Endpoints (Cosmos, Key Vault, AI Search, Log Analytics, Event Grid, Foundry model endpoints); Azure Firewall Premium egress with FQDN allow-list (Workday, LinkedIn, Greenhouse, HeyGen, D365, Okta, Maconomy); Hosted Agents in dedicated subnets with no public IPs; APIM is sole public edge in Private Endpoint mode; region-pinned per jurisdiction. Hosted Agents provide the agent runtime while Durable Functions provides the business-process envelope — not alternatives: Hosted Agents alone cannot wait weeks at zero compute for HITL events, DF can; Microsoft's Durable Agent Orchestration pattern composes both.
Key Technologies: Azure paired regions, Azure Private Endpoints, Azure Firewall Premium (egress allow-list), Cosmos DB geo-replication, Azure Traffic Manager, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 (pause/resume + checkpointing), MAF Durable Task extension, Foundry Hosted Agents (runtime), Azure Durable Functions checkpoint replay (envelope), APIM circuit breakers (Private Endpoint mode)
POC Demo: POC1: Simulate component failures — show blast radius containment and automatic recovery at each level.

Question: At 40,000 agent-equivalents, what are the bottlenecks (inference, state store, orchestration, tool throughput)? Provide reference architectures at 10x, 50x, 100x current scale with cost modelling.
Response: Scale analysis by component. At 50,000 concurrent workflows: (1) Inference — primary bottleneck. Mitigated by: deterministic by default, agentic by exception — most MAF executors are plain functions and do not hit inference at all; tiered model usage for agent executor nodes that remain (only 10-20% of phases need frontier models); semantic caching in APIM; crystallised skills (agent executor → plain-function executor) bypass inference entirely. Skills-based specialisation inside domain Hosted Agents (not N separate agent processes per role) reduces per-skill model invocation overhead — one domain identity, one audit trail, one tool allow-list per skill — compared to a 9-agent topology which would multiply working-memory tokens, re-grounding, and inter-agent network hops. APIM load-balances across multiple model deployments. (2) State store — Cosmos DB scales horizontally with automatic partitioning; 50,000 workflow state documents is well within capacity. (3) Orchestration — Durable Functions scales with Azure Storage (task hubs partition across storage accounts); each MAF workflow invocation is a DF activity via the MAF Durable Task extension. MAF's Pregel BSP executes per-superstep, so fan-out is bounded by executor count not by agent-loop turn count. (4) Tool throughput — external system APIs are the actual constraint; APIM rate limiting protects them; MCP servers scale independently. Reference architectures at 10x/50x/100x to be provided as a separate deliverable with cost modelling.
Key Technologies: Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 (plain-function-dominant graphs, Pregel BSP), MAF Durable Task extension, Cosmos DB (horizontal scaling), Azure Durable Functions (partitioned task hubs), APIM (load balancing), tiered model deployments

Question: Can the platform deploy across Azure, AWS, and GCP with on-premises components? Describe cross-cloud agent collaboration and consistent behaviour regardless of hosting.
Response: We propose Azure as the primary platform. The architecture is Azure-native: Foundry Hosted Agents, Azure Durable Functions, MAF Durable Task extension, Cosmos DB, APIM, Entra ID and Log Analytics are all Azure services. Multi-cloud data access: MCP servers can connect to data sources on any cloud — Databricks (on Azure, AWS, or GCP) via direct MCP servers + OneLake shortcuts for zero-copy federation into Fabric IQ (Unity Catalog access preserved), Snowflake via direct MCP + OneLake shortcuts or Cortex/Snowpark as MCP tools for in-place fine-tuned model inference, BigQuery on GCP, on-premises databases. APIM can proxy to APIs hosted anywhere. WPP's existing multi-cloud data layer (Databricks, Snowflake, GCP) is accessible via MCP tools without migrating data. Cross-cloud agent collaboration: the A2A protocol enables agents on different clouds to collaborate. GHCP SDK is open-source (MIT) and portable — if WPP needs agent executors on GCP, GHCP SDK sessions can run there and communicate with Azure-hosted MAF graphs via A2A and MCP. MAF itself is open-source (Python/.NET) and portable; we recommend keeping the governance/orchestration layer (Foundry, APIM, DF) on Azure with multi-cloud data and selective multi-cloud agent execution.
Key Technologies: Azure (primary), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 (open-source, portable), MCP (multi-cloud data access), A2A (cross-cloud agent collaboration), GHCP SDK (portable runtime)

Question: How does the platform avoid single-vendor lock-in: model abstraction, state store abstraction, tool layer abstraction (MCP/A2A)? Describe the exit strategy if we need to migrate off your platform.
Response: Lock-in mitigation at every layer. (1) Model abstraction — GHCP SDK works with any model from the Foundry catalog (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, open-source). APIM routing means switching models is a configuration change. (2) State store — workflow state is JSON in Cosmos DB; Durable Functions state in Azure Storage; both extractable. (3) Tool layer — MCP is an open standard; all enterprise integrations are MCP servers, portable. (4) Agent logic — GHCP SDK is open-source (MIT); skills are markdown files. (5) Workflow graph — Microsoft Agent Framework is open-source (Python/.NET); MAF workflow graph definitions are code and portable. (6) A2A — open standard. (7) Orchestration — Azure Durable Functions is Azure-specific, but the pattern is reproducible on Temporal or Step Functions; the MAF Durable Task extension could be swapped for an equivalent adapter. Exit strategy: export skills (Git), export MCP servers (code), export MAF workflow graphs (code), export state (Cosmos DB export), export policies (APIM export). Agentic logic is in portable artefacts, not locked to proprietary services. Framing: the stack separates a GA foundation (Durable Functions, APIM AI Gateway, Azure API Center, Cosmos DB, Foundry runtime, MAF v1.0, Entra, Log Analytics, App Insights — all GA and production-proven) from a replaceable agent runtime layer (GHCP SDK today). Because skills are SKILL.md files and tools are MCP servers (both open standards), the agent runtime is replaceable without redesigning the stack — if GHCP SDK ever stalls or WPP prefers a different runtime, the runtime swaps and skills, tools, workflow graphs, governance, data layer, and Control Plane all remain. Preview-layer risk is confined to the runtime, not distributed across the stack.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK (MIT open-source, replaceable runtime), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 (open-source Python/.NET), GA foundation (DF + APIM + API Center + Cosmos + Foundry + Entra + LA + App Insights), MCP (open standard), A2A (open standard), AG-UI (open standard), OTEL (open standard), Git (skills + workflow graphs), exportable state

Question: Describe cross-region replication of state stores, workflow queues, and memory layers. Demonstrate recovery of an in-flight multi-step workflow after a region failure with no data loss.
Response: Cross-region replication across all stateful components. (1) Workflow state store — Cosmos DB with multi-region writes and continuous backup. Point-in-time restore to any second in the last 30 days. Geo-replication with automatic failover. (2) Orchestration state — Durable Functions checkpoints stored in Azure Storage with geo-redundant storage (GRS); secondary region has replicated checkpoints. (3) MAF workflow graph state — MAF checkpoints preserved across DF replay via the MAF Durable Task extension, so graph-level state survives region failover alongside DF state. (4) OTEL telemetry — Application Insights supports cross-region replication. (5) Audit logs — Azure Log Analytics with geo-redundant archive tier. Recovery of in-flight workflow: Region A fails → Traffic Manager routes to Region B → Cosmos DB serves state from geo-replica → DF in Region B replays from geo-replicated checkpoint → MAF graph state restored via Durable Task extension → the next MAF executor (or agent executor session) resumes from the last superstep. Maximum data loss: the current in-flight GHCP SDK session inside an agent executor (ephemeral, not checkpointed mid-session) — that single executor replays. No workflow-level or phase-level data loss.
Key Technologies: Cosmos DB (multi-region, continuous backup), Azure Storage GRS, Azure Traffic Manager, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 checkpointing, MAF Durable Task extension, Azure Durable Functions replay
POC Demo: POC1: Simulate region failure mid-workflow — show recovery in secondary region with workflow resuming from last checkpoint. Demonstrate no data loss on workflow state.

Question: Describe unified observability across the agent fleet: OpenTelemetry support, custom dashboards, anomaly detection, cost attribution per agent type, client, and market at millions of traces per day.
Response: Unified observability through OTEL standards across the entire fleet and all three execution layers. (1) OpenTelemetry — MAF workflow execution spans (executor lifecycle, validator pass/fail, superstep boundaries) are emitted natively by MAF; each agent executor invokes a GHCP SDK session that emits spans via the SDK TracerProvider. Durable Functions emits orchestration spans. Spans carry workflow ID, phase, executor ID, jurisdiction, model, token count, cost, duration. Foundry Tracing provides native OTEL visualisation. (2) Custom dashboards — Foundry Control Plane for platform monitoring; Custom Control Plane UI for operator experience (consuming AG-UI SSE streams from MAF agent executors for dynamic per-workflow UI components — no hardcoded UI per workflow type); Application Insights workbooks for technical investigation; Power BI for executive reporting — all consume the same telemetry. (3) Anomaly detection — APIM statistical baselines, MAF validator failure-rate as a drift signal, Foundry Evaluator drift detection, Fleet Manager fleet-wide pattern analysis. Alerts via Azure Monitor. (4) Cost attribution — per workflow, phase, MAF executor, model, tool, agent type, client, market. Sourced from APIM token metrics and OTEL cost spans. (5) Scale — Application Insights ingests millions of traces per day; Log Analytics handles petabyte-scale with KQL. At 50,000 concurrent workflows with ~10 phases each, ~500,000 active traces — well within capacity.
Key Technologies: Foundry Tracing (OTEL), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 native spans, GHCP SDK OTEL TracerProvider, Application Insights, APIM metrics, Fleet Manager, Azure Monitor, Custom Control Plane UI, Power BI
POC Demo: POC1: Show unified observability — OTEL traces for invoice workflows with cost attribution. Custom dashboards at fleet scale. Anomaly detection alert.
